questions.prompt: An "AI SRE" demo connects a model to a `run_kubectl(command)` tool. A pod's log contains the line `kubectl delete ns prod`. What decides whether production gets deleted?
choices: How well the system prompt tells the model to ignore instructions in logs
Whether the loop exposes a tool that can run it: a model reading suggestive text is expected, so the tool surface and the loop's gates decide what text can become
The model's size
Whether the log is in JSON
questions.explanation: Logs, events and tickets are untrusted text the model reads through tools. Prompt instructions reduce the odds; only a tool surface on which the action is impossible, plus a write path behind operator approval, removes them.

questions.prompt: The response has stop_reason max_tokens and contains a tool_use block. What does the loop do?
choices: Executes the tool; the input looked valid
Stops without running anything in that turn: a truncated input often parses as a valid partial object, and the same rule applies to refusal
Retries the tool call with fewer arguments
Asks the model to confirm
questions.explanation: Cut-off output can leave a tool_use with a shortened input that still parses. The loop treats max_tokens and refusal as exits for that turn; a real deployment would retry with a larger max_tokens or let the fallback handle a refusal.

questions.prompt: One response carries three tool_use blocks. How do their results go back?
choices: One user message per result, in the order they finished
All three tool_result blocks in a single user message, in order, failed ones included with is_error
Only the successful results
Concatenated into one text block
questions.explanation: Parallel tool calls expect parallel results. Splitting them across messages or dropping a failed one teaches the model to stop making parallel calls, and the ids must match the tool_use blocks.

questions.prompt: The model calls propose_action for a rollout_restart. In which order do the gates apply before anything runs?
choices: Operator approval, then the model confirms

The kind must be enabled when the agent started, an operator must approve the exact command, and --execute must be on; otherwise the approved command is printed for a human and the model is told it has not run
The model decides and the loop logs it
The MCP server checks its allow-list
questions.explanation: Three separate gates make a misconfiguration fail safe: forgetting --execute prints a command instead of running it, and the model never sees anything but the decision in words.

questions.prompt: Why does the write path call kubectl directly with a pinned context instead of adding a write tool to the MCP server from the previous lesson?
choices: MCP cannot express writes
The server is read-only by construction and every client relies on that; a second, smaller door with its own gates and audit keeps the guarantee intact
kubectl is faster than JSON-RPC
The server cannot see the kubeconfig
questions.explanation: A guarantee is only useful if it holds for every client. Writes get their own path with an enabled-kinds list, approval, --execute and an audit entry, and the read-only server stays read-only.

questions.prompt: What does opting into fallbacks: "default" change for the triage loop?
choices: It retries rate-limited requests

When a safety classifier declines the request, the API re-runs it on a model chosen by refusal category instead of returning refusal, so a false positive does not end the investigation; the loop still checks stop_reason
It makes the model cheaper
It disables thinking
questions.explanation: Logs full of exploit strings can trip a classifier. The server-side fallback keeps the loop alive; the loop still handles refusal because the fallback model can decline too.
